query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled surface nanostructuring treatment to generate a nanohierarchical layer—comprising gradient nano‐coupled grains interspersed with finely dispersed nanoprecipitates—on a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix will enable adaptive friction interface protection and yield lower friction coefficients and wear rates across the temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: A bulk CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with a conventional, coarse-grained microstructure.
generation.intervention: Apply a surface engineering treatment (such as high-energy shot peening or laser surface treatment) to induce an in situ formation of a graded nanohierarchical microstructure characterized by nano-coupled grains and uniformly distributed nanoprecipitates.
generation.conditions: Sliding tests performed in air with normal loads in the range of 5–20 N and sliding speeds similar to those in benchmark reciprocating tests, over the temperature range from ~25 °C to 800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: A nanohierarchical surface layer containing a gradient in grain size and composition, which at low temperature promotes multiple deformation pathways and at high temperature activates tribochemical oxidation to form a dense, nanocrystalline glaze layer.
generation.mechanism: At room temperature, the nano-coupled grains allow stress to be distributed over multiple deformation modes, minimizing plastic damage and friction. At elevated temperatures, the nanoprecipitates and fine grains promote rapid tribo-oxidation that forms a protective, lubricious glaze layer, thereby reducing adhesive and oxidative wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated CoCrFeNi material, the treated alloy is expected to exhibit a significantly lower coefficient of friction and reduced wear rate—potentially by one to two orders of magnitude—across the entire temperature regime.
generation.baseline: The performance of the as-cast or conventionally processed CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy under similar sliding conditions without the nanostructuring intervention.
generation.boundary: Tested in ambient air with sliding loads of 5–20 N and sliding speeds as per standard tribometer setups; temperature range from room temperature (~25 °C) to 800 °C.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal processing parameters required to reliably produce the desired nanohierarchical layer on the CoCrFeNi surface and the exact quantitative improvement in friction and wear metrics remain uncertain until experimentally verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeNi samples: one set with the surface nanostructuring treatment to induce the nanohierarchical layer, and a control set left in the conventional state. Conduct sliding wear tests over a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C under identical load and sliding speed conditions in air.
measurements: Coefficient of friction (COF) recorded continuously during sliding tests.
Wear rate determined by measuring wear volume using profilometry or microscopy.
Microstructural characterization (e.g., TEM/SEM) before and after tests to confirm the formation and stability of the nanohierarchical layer.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in COF and wear rate—in the order of an order of magnitude improvement relative to the control samples—across the full temperature range, or if the adaptive nanohierarchical layer is not sustained throughout the tests, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. Our work uncovers a practical avenue for tailoring wear properties with multicomponent heterostructures over a wide temperature range.

To summarize, this work proposes a paradigm for the development of ultra-wear-resistant alloys by combining A1 to A3 nano-coupled grains with A2 nanoprecipitates. The designed NiX is capable of activating favorable microstructure evolution and tribo-reaction during sliding, an effect that we refer to as adaptive friction interface protection. Contributing to the roles co-played by nanohierarchical architecture and spatial composition undulation, bulk NiX achieves ultralow wear rate between RT and 800 °C, which heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for any bulk alloys or composites. Such wear response found in the current CCA can be selectively applicable to other alloy systems to achieve pleasing wear resistance.

The tribocorrosion mechanism of the film was analyzed by a linear reciprocating friction machine configured with three electrodes. Si3N4 ceramic grinding balls (Φ 6 mm) were slid for 30 min at a load of 5 N and a frequency of 1 Hz. Prior to formal testing, the sample was immersed in the electrolytic cell with the corrosion solution until the surface potential was stable. The changes in open circuit potential (OCP) and coefficient of friction (COF) were collected in real time throughout the experiment. The wear rate was obtained by the formula w = V/F × S. And the meanings of each physical quantity are as follows: V (mm3) represents wear volume, F (N) represents applied load and S (m) represents sliding distance.
